title: Judges 10:6–18
context: Israel again does evil, serving the gods of many surrounding peoples and abandoning the LORD. He sells them to the Philistines and the Ammonites, who oppress Gilead for eighteen years and cross the Jordan to fight Judah, Benjamin, and Ephraim. When Israel cries out and confesses, the LORD recalls past deliverances and declares that he will save them no more, telling them to cry to the gods they have chosen. Israel confesses again, puts away foreign gods, and serves the LORD, and the text says his soul was grieved for Israel’s misery. The chapter ends with Ammon camped in Gilead and Gilead’s leaders seeking someone to lead them, setting up the story of Jephthah.

verses.text: The children of Israel again did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight, and served the Baals, the Ashtaroth, the gods of Syria, the gods of Sidon, the gods of Moab, the gods of the children of Ammon, and the gods of the Philistines. They abandoned the LORD, and didn’t serve him.
verses.arminianNotes: Israel serves the Baals, the Ashtaroth, and the gods of Syria, Sidon, Moab, Ammon, and the Philistines. Arminian readers see the long list as showing Israel’s widening apostasy, freely chosen despite repeated deliverance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the list as the cycle of Judges reaching a low point, with Israel abandoning the LORD for gods on every side. Both traditions read the verse as a sweeping indictment, ending with the plain statement that Israel did not serve him.

verses.text: The LORD’s anger burned against Israel, and he sold them into the hand of the Philistines and into the hand of the children of Ammon.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD’s anger burns, and he sells Israel to the Philistines and Ammonites. Arminian readers see God’s judgment as a just response to persistent sin, intended to bring his people to their senses and back to him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s sovereign hand handing Israel over in discipline, as in earlier cycles (compare 2:14). Shared ground: the two named oppressors prepare for the stories of Jephthah against Ammon and Samson against the Philistines.

verses.text: They troubled and oppressed the children of Israel that year. For eighteen years they oppressed all the children of Israel that were beyond the Jordan in the land of the Amorites, which is in Gilead.
verses.arminianNotes: The oppressors crush Israel, especially those beyond the Jordan in Gilead, for eighteen years. Arminian readers note the long duration and the suffering it represents for the tribes east of the Jordan.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the length of oppression as a measure of Israel’s stubbornness before crying out. Both traditions read the verse as setting the scene in Gilead, where the next deliverer will come from, under a long and severe affliction.

verses.text: The children of Ammon passed over the Jordan to fight also against Judah, and against Benjamin, and against the house of Ephraim, so that Israel was very distressed.
verses.arminianNotes: Ammon crosses the Jordan to fight Judah, Benjamin, and Ephraim, and Israel is greatly distressed. Arminian readers note that the oppression spreads west, reaching tribes at the heart of the land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the widening distress as God’s discipline pressing harder on his people. Shared ground: the verse explains why Israel is driven to cry out, as the crisis now affects tribes on both sides of the Jordan.

verses.text: The children of Israel cried to the LORD, saying, “We have sinned against you, even because we have forsaken our God, and have served the Baals.”
verses.arminianNotes: Israel cries out and confesses: we have sinned, forsaken our God, and served the Baals. Arminian readers see a real confession, spoken in distress, and note that it names the sin specifically rather than vaguely.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the confession is genuine in its words but tested by the LORD’s response in the following verses. Both traditions read the cry as the familiar turning point in the cycle, now with an explicit admission of guilt.

verses.text: The LORD said to the children of Israel, “Didn’t I save you from the Egyptians, and from the Amorites, from the children of Ammon, and from the Philistines?
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD recalls saving Israel from the Egyptians, Amorites, Ammonites, and Philistines. Arminian readers see God reminding his people of his faithfulness, which makes their repeated unfaithfulness all the more serious.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the list of past deliverances as a covenant lawsuit, setting God’s grace against Israel’s ingratitude. Shared ground: God’s reply begins by recounting his saving acts, which form the basis for the charge that follows.

verses.text: The Sidonians also, and the Amalekites, and the Maonites, oppressed you; and you cried to me, and I saved you out of their hand.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD adds the Sidonians, Amalekites, and Maonites: you cried, and I saved you. Arminian readers note the pattern of crying out and deliverance, now repeated so often that Israel seems to take it for granted.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the Maonites are not clearly identified elsewhere in Judges, and the list may draw on events not recorded in detail. Both traditions read the verse as emphasizing the many times God has already shown mercy.

verses.text: Yet you have forsaken me and served other gods. Therefore I will save you no more.
verses.arminianNotes: Yet you forsook me, so I will save you no more. Arminian readers see a real warning that God’s patience is not to be presumed on, and that he will not simply continue the cycle without a genuine change of heart.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the statement as a solemn rebuke that exposes the shallowness of repentance offered only to escape trouble. Shared ground: the words are meant to confront Israel, and the following verses show that the matter does not end here.

verses.text: Go and cry to the gods which you have chosen. Let them save you in the time of your distress!”
verses.arminianNotes: Go cry to the gods you have chosen. Arminian readers note the irony: Israel chose these gods freely, and the LORD now invites them to test whether those gods can save, as Deuteronomy 32:37–38 also challenges.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the rebuke as exposing the powerlessness of idols, which cannot answer in a time of distress. Both traditions read the verse as stripping away false hopes, leaving Israel with no option but to turn to the LORD alone.

verses.text: The children of Israel said to the LORD, “We have sinned! Do to us whatever seems good to you; only deliver us, please, today.”
verses.arminianNotes: Israel confesses again and submits: do to us whatever seems good to you, only deliver us today. Arminian readers see a deeper repentance, now placing itself entirely at God’s disposal rather than bargaining.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the shift from asking for rescue to accepting whatever God decides, a mark of genuine humility. Shared ground: the second confession goes beyond the first, and both traditions see it as a real turning toward the LORD.

verses.text: They put away the foreign gods from among them and served the LORD; and his soul was grieved for the misery of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Israel puts away foreign gods and serves the LORD, and his soul was grieved for their misery. Arminian readers see God genuinely responding to his people’s repentance, with real compassion toward their suffering.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers affirm God’s real compassion, often reading the language as anthropopathic: it describes his mercy in human terms without implying a change in his eternal purpose. Shared ground: repentance is shown in action, and God’s compassion is real.
verses.keyContrast: Both traditions affirm that God’s compassion toward Israel is real and that He does not change in His character. Classical Arminian readers generally see God’s response as genuinely conditioned on Israel’s free repentance, which He foreknows and to which He responds. Reformed readers generally see Israel’s repentance itself as the fruit of God’s prior grace, and read the language of grief as describing His unchanging mercy in human terms. The difference concerns how repentance and divine relenting relate to God’s eternal purpose.

verses.text: Then the children of Ammon were gathered together and encamped in Gilead. The children of Israel assembled themselves together and encamped in Mizpah.
verses.arminianNotes: Ammon gathers and encamps in Gilead, while Israel assembles at Mizpah. Arminian readers note that the crisis remains unresolved, with two armies facing each other and Israel still lacking a leader for the battle.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God preparing to answer his people’s cry through the deliverer the next chapter introduces. Both traditions note that this Mizpah in Gilead is probably distinct from other places of that name, and its exact location is uncertain.

verses.text: The people, the princes of Gilead, said to one another, “Who is the man who will begin to fight against the children of Ammon? He shall be head over all the inhabitants of Gilead.”
verses.arminianNotes: Gilead’s leaders ask who will begin the fight, promising to make him head over Gilead. Arminian readers note that they look for a leader by offering a reward, a human approach that will shape the story of Jephthah.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the leaders do not ask the LORD whom to choose, though he will still work through the man they find. Shared ground: the chapter ends with a search for leadership, setting up the story of Jephthah in chapter 11.
